analysis.one_liner: Shifts roughly $60 billion from weapons programs to schools, children's health care, and job training.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote — it sat in five House committees and their subcommittees until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut about $60 billion from specific defense and nuclear weapons programs — including the F-22 and F-35 fighter jets, the V-22 Osprey, ballistic missile defense, and space weapons — and spent the money instead on repairing public schools, expanding children's health coverage, job training for unemployed workers, energy efficiency, humanitarian aid abroad, and reducing the deficit. It was referred to five different House committees, then sent to subcommittees, and no committee ever voted on it. It died when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed: school districts repairing crumbling buildings ($10 billion), states covering more uninsured children through CHIP ($10 billion), unemployed and displaced workers getting job training ($5 billion), programs promoting energy efficiency and renewable energy ($10 billion), humanitarian and development programs abroad ($13 billion), medical research ($2 billion), and the Treasury through deficit reduction ($5 billion).

how_it_helps.text: Provides $10 billion to modernize public school facilities; the bill cites GAO estimates that a third of the nation's schools, serving 14 million children, need extensive repair or replacement.
Provides $10 billion for state child health plans (CHIP), expanding health coverage for children.
Provides $5 billion for adult and dislocated worker employment and training under the Workforce Investment Act.
Provides $10 billion for energy efficiency, conservation, and sustainable and renewable energy programs.
Directs $5 billion to deficit reduction and $2 billion to medical research.

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors building the named aircraft, submarines, ships, and missile defense systems, and the national nuclear weapons complex, which would have lost about $60 billion in fiscal 2007 funding. Workers and communities that depend on defense spending would bear some of the job and contract impact.

drawbacks.text: Cutting $8.3 billion from ballistic missile defense, $2.8 billion from the F-22, $2.3 billion from Virginia-class submarines, and other major programs would slow or shrink weapons the Pentagon was actively developing, which critics argued was needed for military capability and jobs in defense-dependent districts.

The bill cuts $14 billion from Department of Energy national nuclear security programs in a single year, a reduction large enough that it could have disrupted the nuclear weapons complex and its workforce rather than only trimming overhead.

Hard-coding exact dollar cuts and reallocations into law removes the flexibility of the annual appropriations process, which is how Congress normally adjusts defense and domestic spending as conditions change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is real and was honestly framed by the bill itself: it names specific weapons programs — including systems the bill calls Cold War leftovers — and directs the money to schools, children's health, and job training with exact dollar amounts. The costs are genuine too: reduced military procurement, pressure on defense-industry jobs, and a blunt one-year cut to the nuclear security budget. Whether the weapons cuts were prudent or reckless depended on one's view of the programs; the bill's own findings argue many were wasteful, but there was no committee hearing or debate to test that case.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to five committees at once, then passed down to subcommittees, and none of them ever voted on it — it quietly expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lynn Woolsey introduced the bill on March 8, 2006, joined by 15 original cosponsors including Reps. Lee, Kucinich, Conyers, and McDermott.
The bill would have cut about $46.5 billion from twelve named Defense Department programs and $14 billion from Department of Energy national nuclear security programs for fiscal 2007.

It would have redirected the money to $10 billion for school modernization, $10 billion for state child health plans, $5 billion for job training, $10 billion for energy efficiency and renewables, $13 billion for humanitarian and development aid, $5 billion for homeland security, $5 billion for deficit reduction, and $2 billion for medical research.

On introduction it was referred to five committees — Armed Services, Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Homeland Security, and International Relations — spreading it across committees with different chairs.

In the following weeks it was referred further to subcommittees on Health, Military Personnel, 21st Century Competitiveness, and Education Reform. No committee or subcommittee ever voted on it, and no version ever reached the House floor before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors and the congressional majority that controlled the committees came out ahead: every named weapons program kept its funding, and the defense and nuclear security budgets were left intact for another year. The proposed school repairs, children's health expansion, and job training never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defense contractors and the House majority

for.name: Rep. Lynn Woolsey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 15 original co-introducers from the House Progressive Caucus wing.

for.name: 38 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; all 38 were Democrats, with no Republican support.

against.name: Duncan Hunter
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral — with the bill's $46 billion in defense cuts squarely in its jurisdiction — and never reported the bill out or held a vote on it.

against.name: House Republican leadership, 109th Congress
against.role: Majority party controlling House committees and the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor at any point in the session.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and there were no Republican cosponsors; Republicans held the House majority and chaired every committee the bill was sent to in 2006.

industries.industry: Defense contractors (fighter, aircraft, submarine, and missile makers)
industries.note: The bill would have cut roughly $46.5 billion from programs these companies build, including the F-22, F-35, V-22 Osprey, Virginia-class submarines, missile defense, and space weapons. The bill died, so the funding continued — the industry kept the money that would have gone to schools and children's health coverage.

industries.industry: Nuclear weapons complex (National Nuclear Security Administration contractors)
industries.note: A $14 billion cut to DOE national security programs would have reduced the budget that sustains the nuclear weapons complex and its contractors. The bill's death preserved that funding.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and energy efficiency sector
industries.note: The bill would have directed $10 billion to energy efficiency, conservation, and renewable energy programs, creating work in that sector. It never passed, so no new funding flowed.
The $10 billion for school facility modernization would have funded building repair and replacement work. The bill never advanced, so none of it was spent.
